Appendix A Benchmark Details A.1 Overall Coverage We evaluate FALCA on five complementary benchmarks that cover diverse forms of search-augmented reasoning. BrowseComp and DeepSearchQA emphasize long-horizon information seeking, requiring persistent retrieval, multi-source evidence aggregation, and answer synthesis. GAIA evaluates general agentic capabilities, including planning, tool use, multimodal understanding, and multi-step reasoning, while xbench-2510 focuses more specifically on end-to-end deep search in the Chinese web environment. WideSearch-en complements these depth-oriented benchmarks by evaluating broad information seeking, where an agent must collect and organize a large number of atomic facts from a wide search space. Together, these benchmarks span constraint-intensive deep search, general tool-augmented reasoning, and broad-coverage information collection, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of search depth, constraint verification, research-state maintenance, and information coverage. A.2 BrowseComp BrowseComp consists of 1,266 open-domain questions designed to evaluate an agent’s ability to persistently browse the web for hard-to-find and entangled information. Although its reference answers are typically short and easily verifiable, they are difficult to obtain through direct lexical matching with the original question. Solving these tasks often requires repeated query reformulation, integration of evidence distributed across webpages, and elimination of plausible candidates that satisfy only part of the given constraints. BrowseComp therefore provides a focused evaluation of persistent retrieval, candidate verification, and constraint-intensive reasoning. A.3 GAIA GAIA is a general-assistant benchmark comprising 466 real-world questions with unambiguous answers. Its tasks require combinations of logical reasoning, web browsing, multimodal information processing, file handling, computation, and external tool use. Unlike benchmarks devoted exclusively to web retrieval, GAIA evaluates whether an agent can identify the operations required by a task, organize them into a coherent multi-step plan, and maintain task-relevant information across heterogeneous interactions. A.4 DeepSearchQA DeepSearchQA contains 900 handcrafted prompts across 17 domains and evaluates whether agents can execute complex, multi-step search plans to produce exhaustive answer sets. Each task is structured as a causal search chain in which later discoveries depend on the successful completion of earlier steps. In addition to retrieving fragmented information from multiple sources, agents must perform entity resolution and deduplication, maintain context over long trajectories, and determine when the open-ended search space has been sufficiently covered. We report F1, which balances the precision of the predicted answer set against its coverage of the reference answers. A.5 xbench-2510 xbench-DeepSearch evaluates end-to-end search capabilities, including planning, retrieval, reasoning, and information summarization. We use xbench-DeepSearch-2510, a refreshed 100-question version designed around the Chinese web environment. Its questions are expert-curated and typically require agents to integrate multiple constraints, distinguish among partially matching candidates, and synthesize evidence into a uniquely verifiable answer. A.6 WideSearch-en WideSearch evaluates broad information seeking rather than deep investigation of a single hidden answer. The full benchmark contains 200 manually curated tasks from more than 15 domains, equally divided between English and Chinese; we evaluate on its 100-question English subset, WideSearch-en. Each task requires the agent to collect a large set of independently verifiable atomic facts and organize them into a structured output. Its primary challenge is therefore to maximize information coverage while avoiding irrelevant, duplicated, or incorrect entries. We report Item-F1, which jointly measures item-level precision and recall over the collected information. Appendix B Baselines We compare FALCA with representative search agents spanning model scales from 4B to 32B parameters. These baselines cover diverse approaches to long-horizon information seeking, including challenging data synthesis, context management, interaction scaling, and agentic reinforcement learning. This comparison evaluates both absolute search performance and parameter efficiency. For external agents, we use results reported in their original papers or official technical reports only when the benchmark version and evaluation metric are compatible with ours; otherwise, the corresponding result is marked as unavailable. B.1 Large-Scale Agents We include four 30B–32B search agents. DeepMiner-32B combines reverse-constructed, high-difficulty search tasks with a dynamic context-window mechanism to support sustained long-horizon interactions. WebDancer-32B develops an end-to-end information-seeking agent through browsing-data construction, trajectory sampling, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. WebSailor-32B targets complex information-seeking tasks through high-uncertainty data construction, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning. Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B integrates agentic mid-training and post-training with scalable automatic data synthesis for long-horizon deep research. B.2 Compact Agents We further compare with four compact search agents. MiroThinker-8B studies interaction scaling, training the model to benefit from deeper and more frequent agent–environment interactions. WebExplorer-8B constructs challenging search tasks through model-based exploration and iterative long-to-short query evolution, followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. LiteResearcher-4B introduces a lightweight virtual search environment to enable scalable and stable agentic RL for deep-research agents. AgentCPM-Explore-4B targets long-horizon exploration at the edge-model scale through model fusion, reward denoising, and contextual information refinement. The two 4B agents provide the most direct parameter-matched comparison with FALCA-4B. Appendix C Implementation Settings Appendix D Prompts The complete prompts used in our experiments are provided in Figures 7 – 13 . We use role-specific prompts to separate hypothesis construction from adversarial verification. The Searcher is instructed to maintain multiple candidate hypotheses, distinguish hard constraints from soft clues, gather URL-grounded evidence, and periodically externalize its research state through update_context . In contrast, the Falsifier follows a contradiction-first protocol: it independently attacks one candidate, checks whether the candidate violates the task constraints or requested answer type, and returns a structured verdict of reject , survive , or uncertain . We additionally use auxiliary prompts for evidence processing, context management, and evaluation. The visit summarization prompt extracts goal-conditioned evidence from webpages while producing a compact summary for later context folding. When the context limit is reached, the context limit prompt requires the Searcher either to serialize the current research state or to terminate with a verified answer. Finally, the answer grading prompt extracts the predicted answer and evaluates its correctness against the reference answer under a standardized format. The five tools support three stages of the propose–falsify research process. First, search and visit provide evidence acquisition. The former executes multiple complementary queries in one call, while the latter retrieves goal-conditioned evidence from one or more webpages. Second, update_context serves as the central research-state transition interface. It serializes the current interaction history into an evidence-grounded context, an explicit constraint list, and a set of candidate hypotheses. When candidate hypotheses are provided, the runtime invokes independent Falsifiers and appends their reports to the refreshed research state, thereby connecting context compression with active falsification. Finally, finish and refute define the terminal actions of the Searcher and Falsifier, respectively. The Searcher uses finish to return a concise answer together with supporting evidence and a confidence estimate. The Falsifier uses refute to return a candidate-level verdict, constraint status, relevant sources, and recommended follow-up searches. Together, these tools provide a structured interface for evidence acquisition, research-state revision, and answer synthesis.
